newsitem.title: ISRAEL: US impatient as Hebron deal eludes Israel, PLO.
newsitem.headline: US impatient as Hebron deal eludes Israel, PLO.

text.p: Despite a sharp prod from Washington, Israelis and Palestinians still seem unable to bridge the remaining gap and strike a deal that would extend self-rule to the West Bank town of Hebron.

The two sides spent another day at the bargaining table on Thursday as police remanded two religious Jews in connection with a shooting spree in the West Bank which landed seven Palestinians in the hospital.

But by the end of the day talk of an imminent summit between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat to seal a Hebron accord had given way to mutual recrimination.

"Apparently the Israelis are having second thoughts about things that have been concluded last week on Hebron," said a PLO official after Palestinian President Yasser Arafat met U.S. envoy Dennis Ross late on Thursday in Gaza.
Arafat told reporters an agreement was near but his spokesman said there would be no meeting between the two leaders before Saturday.

"We will see whether in the next 48 hours an agreement will be reached which will pave the way for an Arafat-Netanyahu meeting. Most probably, there will be no meeting before Saturday, nor an agreement before that day," Nabil Abu Rdaineh told Reuters.
Ross, who has mediated between the two sides for months, later briefed Netanyahu on his talks with Arafat.
The United States pressed Israel and the Palestinians to complete a deal, saying protracted negotiations were fuelling instability and the potential for that it called increased terrorist activity.

In Washington, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said: "They have the capacity to make this deal. It's up to them to do it. They are the only ones who can." Burns called the deal, due to be completed nearly one year ago, "long overdue".

Most of Hebron, where 400 armed Jewish settlers live among 100,000 Palestinians, was to be handed over to Palestinians nine months ago under a 1995 Israeli-PLO peace deal but violence and security concerns have held it up.

Palestinian negotiator Jamil al-Tarifi said the the main dispute now was a PLO demand that Israel commit itself to target dates for further redeployments after Hebron, mostly in rural areas of the West Bank. These redeployments were already agreed in previous peace deals.
Netanyahu's top policy adviser, who early in the day was predicting a summit within hours, later accused Palestinians of stalling at the final hour to squeeze Israel for concessions.
"Well, it's quite clear the stalling is being done by the Palestinian Authority," said adviser David Bar-Illan.
"The most reasonable guess is that they're doing it because they feel that the situation of no agreement favours them and is detrimental to us," he told Israel Radio.
Thursday's talks were conducted in the shadow of the wounding on Wednesday of seven Palestinians in Hebron by an off-duty Israeli soldier.

A magistrate's court ordered Noam Friedman, an orthodox Jew from the West Bank settlement of Maaleh Adumim, held for 10 days on suspicion of attempted murder and sedition and remanded a second suspect, Yuval Jibil, for four days.

Friedman, 22, told investigators he fired his M-16 automatic rifle on Palestinians in an outdoor vegetable market in Hebron to sabotage any transfer of power to Palestinians in Hebron. Other soldiers jumped on Friedman after he began shooting.
A police spokesman said Jibli was suspected of helping Friedman plan the attack but the suspect told the judge he was not involved.
Israel Radio said Friedman told the court he regretted having failed to kill Palestinians in the attack. He protested against being remanded in a "secular court" by a woman judge, the radio said.
